lines.text: Freedom has never simply been given. It was argued for, marched for, and often died for. This is the long fight for human rights, from ancient Babylon to today.
In 539 BCE Cyrus the Great of Persia took Babylon, and a clay cylinder recorded his rule and the return of sacred statues to their temples. Many now see it as an early statement of tolerance.
In 1215, at Runnymede, English barons forced King John to accept Magna Carta. Even a king, it said, was bound by law, and free men were owed a fair trial.
Almost five centuries later, after the Glorious Revolution, the English Bill of Rights tied the crown to Parliament, protected free speech there and banned cruel punishments.
In France, the playwright Olympe de Gouges asked a question the revolution would not answer. She wrote a declaration of the rights of woman, and was sent to the guillotine.
Across the Channel, Mary Wollstonecraft argued that women deserved the same education as men. Her book on the rights of woman made her an early voice of feminism.
Meanwhile William Wilberforce spent decades in Parliament fighting the slave trade, and lived just long enough to hear that slavery itself would end in the empire.
In 1776 thirteen American colonies declared themselves free of Britain, and set down the idea that governments exist to protect the rights of the people.
In 1789 revolutionary France declared that people are born free and equal in rights, a statement that echoed through later bills of rights around the world.
Two years later the United States added ten amendments to its constitution, guarding freedom of speech, religion and the press, and the right to a fair trial.
Born into slavery in New York, Sojourner Truth became a powerful speaker for abolition and for women, and her words still ring out: ain't I a woman?
In 1807, after years of campaigning, Britain banned the slave trade across its empire, though slavery itself went on.
Frederick Douglass escaped slavery in Maryland and became one of its fiercest critics, a writer, an editor and in time an adviser to President Lincoln.
Susan B. Anthony fought for the end of slavery and for women's right to vote. In 1872 she cast a ballot anyway, and was fined for it.
Harriet Tubman escaped slavery, then went back again and again to lead others to freedom along the Underground Railroad. In the Civil War she scouted for the Union.
In 1833 Britain ended slavery in most of its empire. The owners were paid large sums. The freed people received nothing, and were first bound to unpaid work.
In the summer of 1848, women and men met at Seneca Falls in New York and demanded equal rights for women, the vote among them.
In Britain, Emmeline Pankhurst founded a union of women in 1903. Her suffragettes protested, broke windows and starved themselves in prison to win the vote.
In 1861 Tsar Alexander the Second ended serfdom in Russia, freeing tens of millions of peasants, though many stayed poor paying for their land.
Two years later, in the middle of the Civil War, Abraham Lincoln declared the enslaved free in the Confederate states, and Black men could now fight for the Union.
In 1864 nations signed the first Geneva Convention, the beginning of rules for how the wounded, prisoners and civilians must be treated in war.
As the Civil War ended in 1865, the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery throughout the United States.
In 1869 Mahatma Gandhi was born in India. He would lead its struggle against British rule with nonviolent protest, and inspire movements far beyond it.
Eleanor Roosevelt was born in 1884. Long after her years as First Lady, she would lead the committee that wrote the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
In 1888 Princess Isabel signed the Golden Law, and Brazil became the last country in the Americas to end slavery.
Born into a Dalit family, B. R. Ambedkar fought caste discrimination all his life, and chaired the committee that drafted India's constitution.
In 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give women the vote. The rest of the world would take decades to follow.
In France, Simone de Beauvoir would argue that one is not born a woman but becomes one. Her book The Second Sex became a foundation of modern feminism.
Thurgood Marshall, a lawyer born in 1908, would win the case that ended school segregation, and become the first Black justice of the Supreme Court.
Rosa Parks was born in Alabama in 1913. Decades later, a quiet refusal on a Montgomery bus would make her a symbol of the civil rights movement.
In 1918 Nelson Mandela was born in South Africa. He would spend twenty seven years in prison fighting apartheid, and walk out to become president.
In 1920, after decades of campaigning, American women won the right to vote, though many Black women would still be kept from the polls.
Malcolm X, born in 1925, became a powerful voice for Black pride and self-determination, until he was shot dead in New York in 1965.
In 1929 Martin Luther King Jr. was born in Atlanta. The Baptist minister would become the voice of the American civil rights movement.
In 1930 Gandhi walked for three weeks to the sea to make salt against the British tax on it. The world watched, and India rose in peaceful defiance.
Harvey Milk, born in 1930, would become the first openly gay man elected to office in California, before he was murdered in 1978.
Desmond Tutu, born a year later, became the archbishop who spoke out against apartheid, and later led South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission.
John Lewis, born in 1940, led students in the movement, was beaten on the bridge at Selma, and went on to serve in Congress for more than thirty years.
In 1955 Emmett Till, a fourteen year old from Chicago, was lynched in Mississippi. His mother chose an open casket, so the nation would see.
Aung San Suu Kyi, born in 1945, led Myanmar's democracy movement through many years of house arrest, and won the Nobel Peace Prize.
As the Second World War ended, leading Nazis stood trial at Nuremberg for crimes against humanity, the birth of modern international criminal law.
But in 1948 South Africa wrote racial separation into law. Apartheid kept a white minority in power for more than four decades.
That same year the United Nations agreed thirty rights that belong to every person. The Universal Declaration was not a treaty, but it inspired many.
In 1950 Europe went further, with a treaty that lets anyone take their own country to a court of human rights.
In 1954 the United States Supreme Court ruled that separate schools for Black and white children could never be equal.
The next year Rosa Parks was arrested on a Montgomery bus. Black residents walked for a year rather than ride, and won. Martin Luther King became a national leader.
In 1957 nine Black students walked into a white high school in Little Rock, escorted by federal troops.
In 1960 South African police fired on a crowd protesting the pass laws at Sharpeville, killing dozens. The world condemned apartheid, and the government banned its opponents.
In 1961 the Freedom Riders rode buses through the American South to challenge segregation, and were beaten by mobs along the way.
That year in London, Peter Benenson wrote about two students jailed for a toast to freedom, and Amnesty International was born to speak for prisoners of conscience.
In 1963 Betty Friedan wrote about the quiet unhappiness of American housewives, and The Feminine Mystique set off a second wave of feminism.
That summer a quarter of a million people gathered in Washington, and heard Martin Luther King say, I have a dream.
A year later the Civil Rights Act banned discrimination by race, colour, religion, sex or origin, the movement's great legal victory.
In 1965 marchers set out from Selma for the vote. Police attacked them on Bloody Sunday, and the nation turned.
Months later the Voting Rights Act swept away literacy tests and other barriers, and Black voter registration in the South rose sharply.
In April 1968 Martin Luther King was shot dead in Memphis, and riots broke out in more than a hundred cities.
The next summer police raided the Stonewall Inn, a gay bar in New York. Nights of protest followed, and the modern gay rights movement began.
In 1976 schoolchildren in Soweto protested against being taught in Afrikaans. Police opened fire, and the struggle against apartheid reached a turning point.
In 1979 the United Nations agreed a bill of rights for women, a treaty that almost every country has signed.
In 1989 students in Beijing called for reform and an end to corruption. In early June the army cleared Tiananmen Square.
That same year the world agreed on the rights of children, in the most widely ratified human rights treaty in history.
In 1990 the United States banned discrimination against disabled people at work and in public places.
In 1995, at a United Nations conference in Beijing, Hillary Clinton declared that women's rights are human rights, and nations agreed a plan for equality.
Malala Yousafzai, born in Pakistan in 1997, spoke up for girls' schooling. Shot by the Taliban, she survived, and became the youngest Nobel Peace laureate.
In 2001 the Netherlands became the first country to let same-sex couples marry. Many others would follow.
The next year a permanent court opened in The Hague to try genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.
In 2006 the United Nations set out the rights of disabled people in a treaty of their own.
At the end of 2010, protests in Tunisia spread across the Arab world. Leaders fell in four countries, while Syria slid into war.
In 2013 Black Lives Matter rose against police violence, and in 2020 its protests filled streets around the world.
In 2015 the United States Supreme Court made same-sex marriage legal in every state.
Two years later, MeToo spread across social media, as people everywhere spoke about sexual harassment and abuse.
And in 2022, after a young woman died in police custody in Iran, women led protests that the world could not ignore.
Each right won here was once only a demand, and the struggle goes on.
